subsystems.name: Antenna array
subsystems.role: collects faint 1–50 MHz signals; individual elements are simple, but many are needed and they must be physically spread out.
parts: electrically short dipole or monopole elements
ground plane or lunar regolith as reflector

subsystems.name: Low-frequency receiver
subsystems.role: amplifies and digitises a very weak sky signal without adding noise of its own.

subsystems.name: Interference control
subsystems.role: keeps the instrument's own electronics from drowning the signal, since the Moon blocks Earth but not the spacecraft.
parts: solar panels switched off while observing

subsystems.name: Deployment system
subsystems.role: puts antennas on the surface or unfolds them in orbit.
parts: rover or hopping deployer to lay out elements
hinged or inflatable booms (for orbiting arrays)

subsystems.name: Power and thermal
subsystems.role: survives the roughly 14-Earth-day lunar night at about 100 kelvin, when solar power is unavailable.

subsystems.name: Communications relay
subsystems.role: the lunar farside has no line of sight to Earth, so data must be bounced around the Moon.
parts: relay satellite at a lunar libration point

subsystems.name: Data pipeline
subsystems.role: separates the cosmological signal from overwhelmingly brighter foregrounds.

buildSteps.title: Pick the site or orbit
buildSteps.detail: The location must have the Moon's bulk between it and Earth across the whole 1–50 MHz band, with clear sky for the target fields. A farside crater rim or a farside polar orbit both work; a low orbit only works while the Earth is occulted.

buildSteps.title: Design the elements
buildSteps.detail: Dipoles are sized for the longest wavelength of interest, so a 30 MHz array needs elements metres across. They are made as lightweight metal or conductive-film structures that fold or roll for launch.

buildSteps.title: Build a quiet receiver
buildSteps.detail: Amplifiers are chosen for low noise at these frequencies, digitised directly, and the whole chain is enclosed and filtered so that its own emissions fall below the sky noise in the same band.

buildSteps.title: Test on Earth in a radio-quiet place
buildSteps.detail: Prototypes are characterised in shielded chambers and at remote sites away from broadcast transmitters; the ionosphere itself blocks most of this band from the ground, so only the electronics can be tested there, not the science.

buildSteps.title: Engineer for the lunar night
buildSteps.detail: Batteries and radioisotope heater units keep the electronics within their temperature range through two weeks of darkness, and instruments are designed to observe only at night, when the Sun is below the horizon.

buildSteps.title: Land and deploy
buildSteps.detail: For a surface array, a lander touches down on the farside and either hinges out masts or sends a rover to unreel antennas over tens to hundreds of metres. For an orbiting array, small satellites separate and extend their booms.

buildSteps.title: Commission and calibrate
buildSteps.detail: The system observes known radio sources and its own calibration noise to establish gain and bandpass, and maps the local interference environment.

buildSteps.title: Observe and store through the night
buildSteps.detail: The array integrates for weeks or months, recording spectra and storing them until the relay satellite is in view.

buildSteps.title: Relay and reduce the data
buildSteps.detail: Data is forwarded to Earth, then foreground emission from our own galaxy is modelled and subtracted to isolate the faint redshifted 21 cm signature.

prerequisites.why: the first soft landing on the lunar farside was achieved in 2019 and a relay satellite has operated at a lunar libration point since 2018, so both the access and the data path are proven.

a low-frequency instrument has operated from lunar orbit aboard a relay satellite, and a radio spectrometer made the first radio astronomy measurements from the lunar surface in 2024, but neither was an array.
the sought-after signal is many orders of magnitude weaker than the instrument's own digital noise unless the electronics are heavily shielded and powered down during observations.
radioisotope heater units and batteries exist, but keeping a multi-element array alive and functioning through repeated two-week nights has not yet been done at this scale.
galactic synchrotron emission is thousands of times brighter than the cosmological signal, so the analysis depends on calibration and modelling that are still being validated on pathfinder data.
arrays spanning kilometres on the surface, or swarms of free-flying antennas, have been studied but not built.

pathway.milestone: single-antenna pathfinders: a planned farside surface spectrometer, and instruments already flown in lunar orbit and on the surface
pathway.unlocks: a measured map of the real radio environment, plus flight-qualified receivers and antenna technology.

pathway.milestone: a small farside array or a dedicated farside-orbiting constellation of a few tens of elements
pathway.unlocks: the first credible measurement of the global redshifted 21 cm spectrum from the cosmic dark ages.

pathway.milestone: kilometre-scale surface arrays or a large dish built inside a farside crater, both studied as concepts
pathway.unlocks: imaging and tomography of the dark ages, resolving structure rather than just an average signal.

pathway.milestone: expanded interferometric arrays with hundreds to thousands of elements
pathway.unlocks: deep surveys for narrowband artificial emission and precision cosmology, using the Moon as a permanent radio shield.
